title: Branching & Merging
tagline: A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit -- that's the whole trick behind Git's speed.

concept.label: What
concept.text: A branch is a lightweight, movable pointer to a commit; main is just the default one, not special magic.

concept.label: Why
concept.text: Branches let you try something (a feature, a fix) without touching working code until you're ready to combine it.

concept.label: How
concept.text: git branch creates one, git switch (or checkout) moves you to it, git merge combines two.

concept.label: When
concept.text: Any time you start work that might fail, take a while, or shouldn't affect main until it's done.

concept.label: Where
concept.text: Every real project's workflow; the foundation Module 7's pull requests are built on.

mnemonic.label: B.S.M.
mnemonic.text: Branch (create) -> Switch (move) -> Merge (combine) -- the three-step cycle of parallel work

sandboxNote.text: type these into a real repo (reuse the one from Module 1) to see branches actually diverge and merge.

code:
git branch                      # list branches -- you're always on one
git switch -c feature-login     # BRANCH + SWITCH in one command (-c = create)

echo "login code" > login.txt
git add login.txt
git commit -m "Add login feature"   # this commit exists ONLY on feature-login

git switch main                 # back to main -- login.txt is gone here!
git merge feature-login         # MERGE: bring feature-login's commits into main
# now login.txt exists on main too

git branch -d feature-login     # clean up -- the branch's work is safely merged in

cycle.title: Read the concept table once
cycle.text: The one sentence worth remembering: a branch is a pointer, not a copy. That's why creating one is instant even on a huge repo -- there's nothing to duplicate.

cycle.title: Type the code yourself — no copy-paste
cycle.text: Type it, and actually look at your files disappearing and reappearing when you switch branches -- that's not a UI trick, your working directory really is changing.
cycle.hint: If a file you expect isn't there, run git branch first -- you're very likely just on a different branch than you think you are.

cycle.title: Apply it to your own data
cycle.text: Create two branches from main, make a DIFFERENT change to the SAME file on each, then try merging both into main one after another -- you're setting up Module 5's conflict-resolution exercise on purpose.

cycle.title: Reflect & note
cycle.text: What did switching branches actually change on disk? Did any uncommitted work follow you, or get left behind?
cycle.placeholder: e.g. I had an uncommitted edit and Git refused to let me switch branches until I committed or stashed it -- that's when Module 9's git stash started making sense...

cycle.title: Tick off before moving on
checklist: I can explain why a branch is called a "pointer", not a copy.
